resources.string: How bile duct cells modify bile
A schematic view of normal physiology. Structures, timing and moving marks are illustrative, not to scale.
Liver cells called hepatocytes make the initial bile. Small ducts collect it and join larger ducts. This is where cells in the duct lining can change the bile as it flows.
Cholangiocytes are the cells that line bile ducts. Their apical surface faces the lumen, the space that carries bile. Their opposite side faces the surrounding tissue.
One way these cells add bicarbonate to bile is through the exchanger AE2. At the apical surface, it moves bicarbonate out into the lumen in exchange for chloride moving into the cell.
As dissolved particles are added to the lumen, the resulting osmotic gradient can draw water from the tissue side into bile. Water can cross the cell through water channels called aquaporins.
The added water and bicarbonate mix with bile already in the duct. The duct lining modifies bile rather than making it from scratch. Bile can flow onward through the common bile duct to the duodenum.
Evidence: bicarbonate exchange in mouse bile duct cells
Evidence: osmotic water movement in rat bile ducts
